rationale:
Evidence: iteration 0 raced to 26.04 with 0 of 60 development trials finishing. Every trial ended off track, progress was only 0.04 to 0.12, RMS error was about 0.03 m on all three tracks, and max error sat just past the 0.06 m limit. Steering oscillation was low (about 0.07), so the controller is not jittering. The robot drifts off the line steadily and quickly rather than oscillating. The near-identical RMS on all three tracks suggests a constant bias, most likely the fixed left/right motor mismatch that the contract describes. With ki = 0, a steady bias produces a steady offset, which is what the data shows. Iteration 1 was never raced, so I have no evidence on its changes.

Changes:
1. Integral term: ki set to 0.5. The integral is capped at +/-2, so it can add up to about 1 unit of turn (about 350 PWM) to cancel the mismatch without windup risk.
2. Proportional gain: kp raised from 2.0 to 4.0 to give more steering authority per cm of offset.
3. Derivative gain: kd set to 0.6 to damp the faster correction and limit overshoot across the line.
4. Speed: base_speed lowered from 1.6 to 1.3. The robot leaves the line within a fraction of a second, so I want more correction time per unit of distance. This trades some speed against the 3 s finish target, so finishing may be harder, but staying on track is the first requirement.
5. Sensing: sensors widened to x = -0.04 to +0.04 at 0.02 m spacing with 16 mm footprints, so a sensor stays on the 25 mm tape at larger offsets. Weights [-2, -1, 0, 1, 2] keep the signal near 50 times the lateral offset, as before.
6. Geometry otherwise unchanged. The off-track limit stays at 0.06 m for any body width up to 0.18 m, so widening the body gains nothing.

Expected result: lower RMS error from the bias correction, fewer off-track exits, and progress rising well above 0.12 on the oval and s-bend. Completion is possible but not assured. If the robot still leaves early, the next race should show whether the bias or the speed is limiting.
